rationale: B wins because it finds the story inside the evidence instead of inflating the launch into a platform war. Its "Substack says its top creators made over $400M last year — but won't say who or how much each" is a clean reporter-shaped hook with a real proof trail; A's "in the ring with YouTube and TikTok" imports a fight the fact set does not prove. A has useful questions, but its best instincts keep getting undercut by overclaiming headlines like "completes its swap" and "all-in-video media app."
gaps_in_A: "Substack completes its swap from email newsletter to all-in-video media app" overstates the update. Native video does not mean Substack has completed a swap or become all-in-video.
"in the ring with YouTube and TikTok" and "short-form, algorithmic-style feed" import competitor conflict and product mechanics not supplied in the facts.

"The numbers behind Substack's 'struggling platform' reputation don't add up" draws a business-health conclusion from creator earnings and paid subscriptions that do not prove Substack's own profitability or runway.
A misses the cleaner $400M story: the opacity of the aggregate creator-earnings claim and the lack of individual disclosure. It turns that into a shaky contrarian angle instead.
gaps_in_B: "short on funding" overstates the provided fact. The update says public funding struggles, not that Substack is currently short on funding.
"capital-intensive infrastructure" is plausible, but not in the facts. The funding angle should keep that as a question until sourced.
"the same cut now extending over video and podcast monetization" is a little too declarative before confirming whether the 10% subscription cut applies identically to video and podcasts.
